system.name: HD 10180
system.description: A Sun-like star 127 light-years away with six confirmed Neptune-class worlds packed into a tightly ordered system.

hd10180-star.name: HD 10180
hd10180-star.description: HD 10180 is a Sun-like star located 127 light-years from Earth in the southern constellation Hydrus. It is a G-type main-sequence star very similar to the Sun in mass and size, hosting at least six confirmed Neptune-class planets.
hd10180-star.funFact: HD 10180 was discovered to host the most densely packed system of Neptune-class planets known at the time of its 2010 announcement.

hd10180-b.name: HD 10180 b
hd10180-b.description: HD 10180 b is the innermost planet in the system, completing an orbit in just over a day. It is a super-Earth class planet with a mass about 13 times that of Earth, subjected to intense stellar radiation at its very close orbital distance.
hd10180-b.funFact: HD 10180 b's extremely short orbital period of 1.18 days makes it one of the most rapidly orbiting known exoplanets.

hd10180-c.name: HD 10180 c
hd10180-c.description: HD 10180 c is a Neptune-like planet orbiting about 0.064 AU from the star. Its mass is similar to Neptune's but its radius is not well constrained, and it receives an enormous flux of stellar radiation at this close distance.
hd10180-c.funFact: The HD 10180 system's inner planets are packed into a remarkably compact region, with all six fitting within the orbit of Mars around our Sun.

hd10180-d.name: HD 10180 d
hd10180-d.description: HD 10180 d is another Neptune-class world in the system, completing an orbit every 16 days. It sits in a region where the stellar flux is comparable to that received by Mercury in our Solar System.
hd10180-d.funFact: All six HD 10180 planets were discovered using the HARPS spectrograph in Chile, which measured tiny Doppler shifts in the star's spectrum.

hd10180-e.name: HD 10180 e
hd10180-e.description: HD 10180 e is one of the most massive planets in the system with about 25 Earth masses. Orbiting at 0.27 AU, it receives roughly the same stellar flux as Venus does from the Sun.
hd10180-e.funFact: HD 10180 e's mass is intermediate between Neptune and Saturn, placing it in the 'super-Neptune' category that has no equivalent in our Solar System.

hd10180-f.name: HD 10180 f
hd10180-f.description: HD 10180 f is an ice giant-class planet orbiting in the system's outer middle region with a period of about 123 days. It is one of the most massive planets in the system and would appear as a large blue-green world.
hd10180-f.funFact: HD 10180 f orbits in a region analogous to Venus's distance from the Sun, receiving moderate stellar energy — yet it is likely a gas-dominated world.

hd10180-g.name: HD 10180 g
hd10180-g.description: HD 10180 g is the outermost known planet in the system, completing one orbit roughly every 1.65 years. It orbits beyond the snow line of the system, where water ice is stable, and may be a large ice giant or gas dwarf.
hd10180-g.funFact: HD 10180 g's distance from its star is similar to Mars's distance from the Sun, making it the most 'habitable zone-adjacent' planet in the system.
